title: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
summary: Why threads see memory operations in different orders, and how the C++/Rust model tames it: Relaxed, Release/Acquire, SeqCst, fences, and what each costs on x86-64 and ARM64.
outcomes: Explain why the store buffering test can end with both reads 0 on x86, and what sequential consistency would forbid
Explain what Relaxed guarantees (atomicity and one modification order per variable) and what it does not
Trace a happens-before chain through a Release store and an Acquire load, including release sequences
Decide when SeqCst or a fence is required, using the flag handshake and Arc's reference count as examples
Map each ordering to x86-64 and ARM64 instructions and pick the weakest correct ordering for common patterns

lessons.title: Why two threads can disagree about what happened first

blocks.md:
In the prerequisite course you used atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS) to make a single read-modify-write indivisible. That solves one problem: two threads cannot both increment a counter and lose an update. It leaves a second problem open: in what order do *other* threads see a thread's memory operations?

Both the compiler and the processor reorder memory operations whenever a single thread cannot tell the difference. Mara Bos's example: a compiler may turn `*a += 1; *b += 1; *a += 1;` into `*a += 2; *b += 1;`, and a CPU may finish the write to `b` first because `b` was in cache while `a` was not. The thread itself sees the same final result either way.

The trouble is that these "invisible" transformations are judged one thread at a time. Another thread watching `a` and `b` can see the changes in an order the source code never wrote.

The intuitive model is **sequential consistency** (SC), defined by Leslie Lamport in 1979: the result of any execution is the same as if the operations of all processors ran in *some* single sequential order, with each processor's operations appearing in that order as its program lists them. In other words, an interleaving. Real multicore hardware does not give you SC by default.

blocks.prompt: Store buffering test (called SB). Memory starts at x = 0, y = 0. Thread 0 runs `x = 1; r1 = y;` and thread 1 runs `y = 1; r2 = x;`. Under some interleaving of these four steps, can both threads read 0, so r1 = 0 and r2 = 0?
blocks.reveal:
Under sequential consistency, **no**. Whichever operation goes first in the interleaving is a write, so the second thread's read sees 1. Enumerating all 6 interleavings gives (r1, r2) = (0, 1) once, (1, 0) once and (1, 1) four times.

On a real x86 machine, **yes**. Sewell et al. list exactly this program and state that both reads returning 0 is an allowed final state on modern Intel and AMD multiprocessors. The next figure shows why.

blocks.title: SB test: which (r1, r2) outcomes are reachable

scenes.caption: Sequential consistency: all 6 interleavings of the 4 operations, counted by outcome. (0, 0) never happens, because the first operation in any interleaving is a write.

Simplified x86-TSO model (each store may be delayed past the same thread's later load): 24 executions, and now every outcome appears 6 times, including (0, 0). These count model executions, not how often each outcome shows up on real hardware.
Same model, but each store is a SeqCst store compiled to xchg, which drains the buffer before the load. Back to the 6 SC interleavings: (0, 0) is gone.

blocks.title: How a store buffer produces r1 = r2 = 0

scenes.caption: Simplified x86-TSO machine (Sewell et al.): each hardware thread has a FIFO store buffer in front of shared memory. Both locations start at 0.
Core 0 executes x = 1. The write goes into its own store buffer so the core does not stall; memory still holds x = 0.
Core 1 does the same with y = 1. Both writes now sit in private buffers that the other core cannot see.
Core 0 reads y. Its own buffer has nothing for y, so it reads memory and gets 0.
Core 1 reads x and also gets 0. Each core saw its own write as done but missed the other's.
Later the buffers drain and memory holds x = 1, y = 1. No interleaving explains (0, 0): each store was effectively reordered after the same thread's later load.
The fix on x86: MFENCE, or a LOCK'd instruction such as xchg, flushes the thread's store buffer, so the write reaches memory before the following load runs.

blocks.md:
x86 is the gentle case. The x86-TSO model (total store order) allows only one visible reordering: a store being delayed past a later load to a different address. ARM64 is **weakly ordered**: the processor may reorder any two memory operations to different addresses unless told otherwise. Other architectures go further still: on some, two stores from one core can become visible to two other cores in different orders.

The compiler adds its own reordering on top, on every architecture. Turning optimizations off does not remove it all, and it does nothing about the CPU.

Instead of exposing every chip's rules, C++11 and Rust define an abstract **memory model**. Each atomic operation takes an ordering argument, and the compiler must emit whatever instructions make that promise true on the target:

- Rust: `std::sync::atomic::Ordering::{Relaxed, Release, Acquire, AcqRel, SeqCst}`. The Rust docs state its orderings are the same as C++20's.
- C++: `std::memory_order_relaxed`, `_consume`, `_acquire`, `_release`, `_acq_rel`, `_seq_cst`. Consume is deprecated in C++26 and Rust leaves it out.

The rest of this course is about what each one promises.

A **data race** is two accesses to the same location from different threads, at least one a write, at least one non-atomic, with no happens-before relation between them. In both C++ and Rust it is undefined behavior, not just a stale read. Orderings are how you create the happens-before relations that rule races out.
Reordering is invisible to the thread that does it and visible to every other thread. Memory orderings are a portable contract about which reorderings other threads are allowed to observe.

blocks.question: On an x86 machine the SB test (x = 1; r1 = y in one thread, y = 1; r2 = x in the other) sometimes ends with r1 = 0 and r2 = 0. What is the best explanation?
options: The cache coherence protocol lost one of the writes
Each core's store sat in its store buffer while the same core's later load read the old value from memory
The two threads ran on the same core, so they could not see each other
x86 reorders every pair of memory operations freely
blocks.explain: Both writes eventually reach memory, so nothing was lost. x86-TSO only allows a store to be delayed past a later load, which is exactly what the store buffer does. Threads time-sliced on one hardware thread share one store buffer, so they would not produce it (two hyperthreads of one core have separate buffers and can), and x86 does not reorder loads with loads or stores with stores.

blocks.question: A colleague says: "Our lock-free queue misbehaves in release builds, so we will ship it compiled with optimizations off." Why does this not make it correct?
options: Debug builds use different atomics
It does: without optimization the compiler emits code in source order and the bug disappears
The CPU can still reorder memory operations, and the compiler still may perform some transformations
Optimization level only affects speed, never ordering
blocks.explain: Mara Bos lists this as a myth: disabling optimization does not disable every compiler transformation, and it does nothing about store buffers, pipelining or other CPU reordering. The fix is to use the right orderings.

lessons.title: Relaxed: one agreed history per variable, nothing more

blocks.md:
The memory model never talks about caches or instruction order. It defines a relation called **happens-before** and promises only what follows from it. Two basic rules:

- Within one thread, every operation happens-before the next one in program order (the C++ term is *sequenced-before*).
- Between threads, happens-before only appears in specific cases: spawning a thread, joining it, unlocking then locking a mutex, and atomic operations with non-relaxed orderings.

If no chain of happens-before links connects two operations, the model gives no order between them.

`Relaxed` is the weakest ordering, and on its own it never creates a cross-thread happens-before. What it still guarantees:

1. **Atomicity**: the operation is indivisible, so a `fetch_add` never loses an update.
2. **A total modification order per variable**: all writes to one atomic variable form a single sequence that every thread agrees on. A thread's successive reads of that variable can only move forward through it.

It guarantees nothing about how operations on *different* variables appear to other threads.

blocks.caption: From Rust Atomics and Locks, ch. 3. X's modification order is 0, then 5, then 15.

blocks.title: Reads must move forward through one variable's history

scenes.caption: Only one thread writes X, so its modification order is 0, 5, 15. Every thread agrees on this order, even with Relaxed.
Output 0 0 5 15: each read is at the same position or later than the previous one. Allowed.
Output 0 15 15 15 is also allowed: the reader jumped past 5 and simply never saw it.
Output 0 5 0 15 is impossible: the third read would move backward from 5 to 0 in X's modification order.
0 0 10 15 is impossible too: 10 never appears in X's history. Of the 81 ways to print four values from {0, 5, 15}, only the 15 non-decreasing ones can occur.

blocks.prompt: Now split the writer in two: thread a1 does `X.fetch_add(5, Relaxed)` and thread a2 does `X.fetch_add(10, Relaxed)`, while hundreds of reader threads print X. One reader prints 10. Can any other reader print 5?
blocks.reveal: **No.** The modification order is either 0, 5, 15 or 0, 10, 15, and every thread agrees on which one happened. A reader seeing 10 proves it was 0, 10, 15, so the value 5 never existed. Relaxed gives you this agreement per variable, for free.

blocks.md:
The weakness shows up as soon as two variables are involved. Mara's example: thread a does `X.store(10, Relaxed); Y.store(20, Relaxed);` and thread b does `let y = Y.load(Relaxed); let x = X.load(Relaxed);`. Thread b may print `x = 0, y = 20`: it saw the second store but not the first, even though no single interleaving produces that.

The classic victim is **message passing** (MP): one thread writes data, then sets a ready flag; another waits for the flag, then reads the data.

blocks.title: Message passing with Relaxed: data = 123; ready = 1

scenes.caption: Sequential consistency (and also the x86-TSO hardware model): 6 executions. Seeing the flag set but stale data, the last bar, never happens.
Simplified weak (ARM64-like) model where each thread may reorder accesses to different addresses: 24 executions, and ready 1 with data 0 appears 6 times.
Careful with the first scene: x86 hardware would not reorder these, but the compiler still may, because Relaxed permits it. Correct code cannot rely on x86 being gentle.

blocks.md:
So when is Relaxed enough? When the atomic variable *is* the whole message and no other memory depends on it. The cppreference example: 10 threads each do `cnt.fetch_add(1, memory_order_relaxed)` 1000 times, and after joining them the main thread always prints 10000. The joins provide the happens-before; the increments only need atomicity.

Other good fits: statistics counters, ID generators, and incrementing a reference count (Rust's `Arc::clone` uses `fetch_add(1, Relaxed)`).

Myth: "Relaxed writes may take ages to show up, and SeqCst makes them visible sooner." The memory model says nothing about timing at all, only about order. A stronger ordering does not make data travel faster; it may even slow your program down.

One theoretical wrinkle: with Relaxed, cyclic reasoning such as thread 1 copying y into x while thread 2 copies x into y could, under a literal reading of the formal rules, produce **out-of-thin-air** values like 42 from nothing. cppreference states C++14 and later forbid such circular results, while Mara Bos notes that formalizing this precisely is still an open problem. Real compilers and CPUs do not produce them.

blocks.question: Ten threads each run `counter.fetch_add(1, Relaxed)` 1000 times; then main joins all ten and reads the counter. What does main see?
options: Exactly 10000
Any value from 1000 to 10000, since Relaxed does not order the increments
10000 on x86 but possibly less on ARM64
Undefined behavior, because Relaxed operations race
blocks.explain: Each fetch_add is atomic, so none are lost, and all of them sit in one modification order. Joining a thread creates happens-before from everything it did to the code after the join, so main reads the final value. Relaxed is not a race: races need a non-atomic access.

blocks.question: A thread writes a 4 KB config buffer with plain writes, then does `READY.store(true, Relaxed)`. A reader spins until `READY.load(Relaxed)` is true and then reads the buffer. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: the reader saw true, so it must also see the buffer
The store of true might never become visible
Relaxed creates no happens-before, so the reader can see stale buffer contents and the buffer accesses are a data race
AtomicBool cannot be used with Relaxed
blocks.explain: Reading true from a relaxed store says nothing about other memory. The buffer writes and reads are not ordered by happens-before, which is a data race and undefined behavior. The fix is Release on the store and Acquire on the load (next lesson).

lessons.title: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads

blocks.md:
**Release** applies to stores and **Acquire** to loads. The rule, from cppreference and the Rust docs: if an Acquire load reads the value written by a Release store, the store **synchronizes-with** the load. Then everything that happened-before the store also happens-before everything after the load.

For read-modify-write operations (swap, fetch_add, compare_exchange), Acquire applies to the load half and Release to the store half; `AcqRel` gives both. The Rust docs warn that Release on an RMW makes its load part Relaxed, and Acquire makes its store part Relaxed.

blocks.caption: Happens-before is the transitive closure of sequenced-before (program order within a thread) and synchronizes-with (a Release write read by an Acquire read). This is cppreference's C++26 form, where consume no longer adds a separate case.
Adapted from Rust Atomics and Locks, ch. 3. DATA can be non-atomic because happens-before keeps its write and read from ever being concurrent.

blocks.title: The happens-before chain that makes DATA safe

scenes.caption: Producer thread (left): the plain write to DATA is sequenced-before the Release store, simply because it comes first in program order.
Consumer thread (right): the Acquire load that returns true is sequenced-before the read of DATA.
The Acquire load read the value written by the Release store, so the store synchronizes-with the load. This is the only cross-thread edge.
Chaining the three edges: the write of 123 happens-before the read of DATA. The read cannot be concurrent with the write, so it is not a race and must see 123.
If the load had returned false, no synchronizes-with edge exists and nothing is promised. That is why the consumer loops until it actually reads true.

blocks.md:
A practical way to picture it, with the caveat that the formal rule is happens-before, not instruction order:

- A **Release** store is a one-way barrier: no memory operation before it may be moved after it.
- An **Acquire** load is the mirror image: no memory operation after it may be moved before it.

That is exactly what a mutex needs. Lock with an Acquire operation (for example `compare_exchange(false, true, Acquire, Relaxed)`) and unlock with `store(false, Release)`. Every unlock then happens-before the next successful lock, so critical sections never overlap.

blocks.prompt: In the message-passing test, suppose only *one* side is upgraded: the flag store uses Release but the flag load stays Relaxed. In the simplified weak model, is "ready 1, data 0" still possible?
blocks.reveal: **Yes.** Enumerating the simplified ARM64-like model: with Release on the store only, 1 of 12 executions still shows ready 1, data 0, because the reader's two loads can be swapped. With Acquire on the load only, the writer's two stores can be swapped, and again 1 of 12 executions shows it. With both, 0 of 6. Synchronization is a pair: one Release, one Acquire, on the same variable.

blocks.md:
"Reads the value written by the store" needs care when the same value is written more than once. Each write is a separate event in the variable's modification order, so the question is *which* write you read.

There is one extension. A **release sequence** headed by a Release write continues through any read-modify-write operations that follow it in the modification order, whatever their ordering. An Acquire load that reads a value written by any of those RMWs still synchronizes-with the head. Before C++20, later plain stores by the same thread also extended the sequence; C++20 removed that case, and Rust follows C++20.

blocks.title: Which release does an Acquire load synchronize with?

scenes.caption: Modification order of one atomic (Mara Bos's example): init 0, Release store 7, Relaxed fetch_add, Release fetch_add, Release store 7, Relaxed swap to 10.
An Acquire load reads 9. The fetch_adds at 2 and 3 are RMWs, so 9 is part of the release sequence headed by the store at 1, and also the one headed by 3. The load synchronizes with both.
An Acquire load reads 10, written by a Relaxed swap. The swap is an RMW following the Release store at 4, so the load synchronizes with 4.
But not with 1 or 3: the plain store at 4 is not an RMW, so it breaks the chain. Reading 7 alone is ambiguous: it could be the write at 1 or the one at 4.

blocks.caption: Lazy initialization through a pointer (Rust Atomics and Locks, ch. 3). Release publishes the initialized Data; Acquire on both the load and the failure path lets every reader see it.

blocks.md: There is no "acquire store" or "release load". Release only affects stores and Acquire only affects loads; SeqCst cannot create them either. A Release store and a Release store never synchronize with each other.

C++ also has `memory_order_consume`: a cheaper Acquire that only orders operations that *depend on* the loaded value, such as dereferencing a loaded pointer. It proved too hard to implement, because compilers optimize dependencies away (`x + 2 - x` becomes `2`). Compilers simply treat it as Acquire, C++26 deprecates it, and Rust never exposed it.

Synchronization needs a pair on the same atomic: a Release (or stronger) write and an Acquire (or stronger) read that observes that write or its release sequence. Then everything before the write is visible after the read.

blocks.question: In `get_data`, someone changes the compare_exchange failure ordering from Acquire to Relaxed. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, because failure means no store happened, so ordering is irrelevant
The losing thread uses the winner's pointer without synchronizing with the Release that published it, so it may read uninitialized Data
The compare_exchange may now succeed twice
It only affects performance on x86
blocks.explain: On failure the operation still loads the winner's pointer, and that pointer is then dereferenced. Without Acquire on that load there is no happens-before from the winner's initialization, so the read of Data is a data race. Mara Bos uses Acquire for exactly this reason.

blocks.question: A spin lock is implemented as `while LOCKED.swap(true, Acquire) {}` ... critical section ... `LOCKED.store(false, ORD)`. Which ORD is the weakest correct choice?
options: Relaxed
Acquire
SeqCst, because unlocking must be globally visible
Release
blocks.explain: The unlock must publish the critical section's writes to the next locker. That needs a Release store paired with the Acquire swap. Acquire is not even allowed on a plain store, Relaxed creates no happens-before, and SeqCst works but promises far more than needed.

lessons.title: SeqCst, fences, and when you need one global order

blocks.md:
**SeqCst** (sequentially consistent) includes everything Acquire gives loads and Release gives stores, plus one more promise: all SeqCst operations in the program form a **single total order** that every thread agrees on, consistent with each variable's modification order.

Acquire and release are about pairs. They never create a global order across *different* variables. The pattern that needs one is: write my flag, then read someone else's flag.

blocks.prompt: Two threads each try to enter a critical section. Thread A runs `A.store(true, Release); if !B.load(Acquire) { enter }`. Thread B runs the mirror image. Can both threads enter?
blocks.reveal: **Yes.** This is the SB test from lesson 1 in disguise. Release only stops *earlier* operations from moving after the store, and Acquire only stops *later* ones from moving before the load. Nothing stops the store from moving after the load, so both loads can read false. Making all four operations SeqCst forbids it, because the first of the four in the single total order is a store, and the other thread's load must see it.

blocks.title: Flag handshake: executions where both threads read false

scenes.caption: Simplified weak (ARM64-like) model, 24 executions each. With Relaxed, 6 of 24 executions have both loads reading false, so both threads enter.
Release on the stores and Acquire on the loads does not help: still 6 of 24, because a store may still be ordered after the next load.
SeqCst on all four operations: they cannot be reordered with each other, so only the 6 sequentially consistent interleavings remain, and none of them has both loads false.

blocks.md:
Mara Bos's version of this pattern guards a non-atomic `String` S: each thread does `MY_FLAG.store(true, SeqCst)`, then pushes to S only if `!OTHER_FLAG.load(SeqCst)`. Possibly neither thread pushes, but never both. Bos notes that virtually all real uses of SeqCst look like this: a store that must be globally visible before a later load on the same thread.

cppreference gives the other classic: two writers set x and y, and two readers check them in opposite orders. Only SeqCst guarantees the readers cannot disagree about which write came first.

SeqCst only orders SeqCst operations. As soon as Acquire, Release or Relaxed operations take part, the global guarantee can fail in surprising ways. C++20 revised the SeqCst rules after Lahav et al. showed the old ones could not be soundly compiled to POWER; under the current rules the total order may disagree with happens-before when orderings are mixed. If you need the total order, make every participating operation SeqCst.

**Fences** separate the ordering from the access. `std::sync::atomic::fence(order)` in Rust, `std::atomic_thread_fence(order)` in C++.

- `fence(Release)` followed by a Relaxed store acts like a Release store.
- A Relaxed load followed by `fence(Acquire)` acts like an Acquire load.
- A release fence synchronizes with an acquire fence if any atomic store after the first is read by any atomic load before the second.

One fence can cover many variables, and it can be conditional: only pay for Acquire on the path that actually uses the data.

blocks.title: Arc drop: Release on every decrement, Acquire only at zero

scenes.caption: Two Arcs share the data, so the strong count is 2. Thread A has finished using the data and drops its Arc.
A's fetch_sub with Release publishes all of A's earlier uses of the data. It returns the old value 2.
Other owners remain, so A returns. No acquire is needed: A will not touch the data again.
Later, thread B drops the last Arc. Its fetch_sub returns 1, so B must destroy the data.
The Acquire fence pairs with A's Release decrement, since B's fetch_sub read a value in that release sequence. All of A's uses now happen-before the destruction.
Only now is it safe to free the data. The common path (count not yet 1) never pays for the Acquire.

blocks.md:
The source comment in Rust's `Arc` explains the same reasoning, citing the Boost documentation: any access through a reference must happen-before the deletion, which takes a Release after dropping a reference and an Acquire before deleting. The comment also notes ThreadSanitizer does not understand fences, so TSan builds use an Acquire load instead.

A `fence(SeqCst)` is both an acquire and a release fence and also joins the single total order. But a SeqCst *operation* cannot be split into a Relaxed operation plus a SeqCst fence, because only the fence enters the total order.

`compiler_fence` (Rust) and `atomic_signal_fence` (C++) only restrict the compiler, not the CPU. They are for code that interrupts the same thread, such as a signal handler or an embedded interrupt. Between two threads on different cores they are not enough.

blocks.question: Why does `Arc::drop` use Release on every `fetch_sub`, rather than only on the one that reaches zero?
options: Because Release makes the decrement faster on x86
Because no thread knows in advance whether its decrement is the last, and every non-final owner's uses must happen-before the deletion
Because fetch_sub cannot be Relaxed
Because SeqCst is required for reference counts
blocks.explain: Whichever thread frees the data needs a happens-before edge from every other owner's last use. Each non-final owner provides that by releasing on its decrement; the final owner acquires (via the fence) before deleting. The Acquire is only needed by the one thread that sees old == 1.

blocks.question: You replace `X.store(1, SeqCst)` with `fence(SeqCst); X.store(1, Relaxed)`. Is that equivalent?
options: Yes, a SeqCst fence plus a Relaxed store is exactly a SeqCst store
Yes, but only on x86
No: the fence is in the SeqCst total order but the store is not, so other SeqCst operations need not agree on where the store sits
No: fences can only be used with loads
blocks.explain: Mara Bos notes this explicitly: only the fence takes part in the single total order, not the atomic operations around it, so a SeqCst operation cannot be split into a relaxed operation and a fence. Release and Acquire can be split that way; SeqCst cannot.

lessons.title: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing

blocks.md:
What do the orderings cost? It depends on what the hardware gives for free. The mappings below come from the Cambridge table of C/C++11 mappings and from compiled Rust in Rust Atomics and Locks, ch. 7.

**x86-64.** Every ordinary load already behaves as Acquire and every ordinary store as Release, because x86-TSO only delays stores past later loads. So Relaxed, Acquire and Release loads and stores are all plain `mov`. A SeqCst store becomes `xchg` (implicitly locked, so it drains the store buffer); a SeqCst load stays `mov`.

blocks.title: What each ordering compiles to (columns: Relaxed, Acq/Rel, SeqCst)

scenes.caption: Loads and stores at each ordering. On x86-64, the only column with a different instruction is the SeqCst store.
On ARM64, Acquire loads use ldar and Release stores use stlr. Relaxed uses ordinary ldr and str, so it is genuinely cheaper there.
ldar and stlr are never reordered with each other, so they already satisfy SeqCst. On ARM64, SeqCst loads and stores cost the same as Acquire and Release.
Fences: on x86-64, Acquire, Release and AcqRel fences emit no instruction and SeqCst emits mfence. On ARM64, Acquire is dmb ishld and the others are dmb ish.

blocks.md:
This asymmetry has a nasty consequence. Using Relaxed where Release or Acquire is required is a bug, but on x86-64 the hardware happens to provide those guarantees anyway. The bug only shows when the compiler reorders, or when the code runs on a weakly ordered CPU.

Mara Bos demonstrates it: four threads each take a spin lock, increment a counter non-atomically and unlock, one million times each, with the lock's orderings wrongly set to Relaxed (plus a `compiler_fence` so only the CPU can reorder). The correct total is 4,000,000.

blocks.title: Lost increments with a Relaxed spin lock (expected total 4,000,000)

scenes.caption: x86-64 printed 4,000,000 every time: acquire and release come for free, so the wrong orderings go unnoticed. An Android phone and a Raspberry Pi 3 (both ARM64) also printed 4,000,000.
An Apple M1 printed 3,988,255, 3,982,153 and 3,984,205: between 11,745 and 17,847 increments lost, an average of 0.38%. The weakly ordered core let critical sections overlap.

blocks.md:
Note what the middle bars say: some ARM64 chips did not show the bug either. Passing tests on your hardware proves little; correctness has to come from the happens-before reasoning.

A decision guide for picking orderings, from the patterns in this course:

- Counter, statistic, ID generator, or a flag with no data attached: `Relaxed`.
- Publishing data through a flag or pointer: `Release` store, `Acquire` load (and Acquire on the CAS failure path if it reads the pointer).
- Locks: `Acquire` when taking, `Release` when releasing.
- Reference counts: `Relaxed` increment, `Release` decrement, `Acquire` fence when it hits zero.
- Store my flag then read yours (Dekker-style): `SeqCst` on all of them, or SeqCst fences.

Start from the happens-before edges your algorithm needs, then pick the weakest ordering that creates each one. Mara Bos suggests treating SeqCst as a warning sign in review: it claims dependence on the order of every SeqCst operation in the program, which is much harder to verify than a single Release/Acquire pair.

`volatile` is not an ordering. In standard C++, volatile accesses are not atomic and do not order other memory, so they cannot be used for synchronization between threads. (MSVC gives volatile acquire/release semantics by default on x86 targets; that is a compiler extension, not the language.)

blocks.question: Code using `Relaxed` for a ready flag passes millions of test runs on x86-64 CI but corrupts data on an ARM64 server. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
options: ARM64 has a broken cache coherence protocol
The code was always wrong: x86-64 gives acquire/release ordering to plain loads and stores, which hid the missing Release/Acquire
x86-64 runs Relaxed operations as SeqCst, so the code is correct on x86-64 and only ARM64 needs a fix
The ARM64 compiler has a bug
blocks.explain: The memory model never promised ordering for Relaxed. x86-TSO happens to prevent the message-passing reordering, but the compiler could still reorder the operations even there. The fix is a Release store and an Acquire load, which costs nothing extra on x86-64.

blocks.question: On x86-64, which of these Rust operations compiles to a different instruction than its Relaxed version?
options: x.load(SeqCst)
x.load(Acquire)
x.store(1, SeqCst)
x.store(1, Release)
blocks.explain: Only the SeqCst store changes: it becomes xchg so that it cannot be delayed past later loads. SeqCst loads stay mov, because the cost is placed on the store side. Mixing the two possible conventions across compilers would break programs, which is why the mapping table recommends the store-side one.

blocks.question: A shutdown flag is set by one thread and polled by workers, which simply exit their loop when they see it. No other data is passed through the flag. Which ordering fits?
options: SeqCst, to make sure workers see it quickly
Release store and Acquire load
Relaxed
AcqRel on both store and load
blocks.explain: The flag carries no other data, so no happens-before edge is needed: Relaxed gives atomicity, and the model says nothing about speed anyway. If the workers had to read results or config written before the flag, you would upgrade to Release and Acquire. AcqRel is only for read-modify-write operations.
